title: 6.2.3 Legend, scale bar and north arrow
text:
North arrow
The last item type discussed here is the north arrow. When you add a north arrow, QGIS adds an image of an arrow to your layout. You can replace this image with any other: QGIS offers a wide range of arrow images in its SVG library (SVG browser), but in principle you can choose any image at all, for example one from your computer.

What makes a north arrow useful is that its rotation can be linked to a map item. Under Image Rotation, make sure that Sync with map is ticked and choose the map it should follow. For example, if you rotate the map 90° clockwise (so that west is at the top), the north arrow turns too and points to the right instead of up.
Under North alignment, you choose where the arrow should point to: Grid North (the direction of the map’s vertical grid lines) or True North (the direction of the geographic North Pole).






On smaller-scale maps the direction of true north can differ substantially from place to place. In that case, a single north arrow is an approximation: it is only correct for the centre of the map. While grid north can diverge from true north, it is the same everywhere on the map.

title: 6.3 Composition and export
text: On the previous pages, you learned how to configure the items on your map. This section covers the layout as a whole: the layout page itself, the export of your map, and some general tips for designing a map.

title: 6.3 Composition and export
text:
The layout page

Size
By default, a new layout page is A4 landscape (29.7 cm wide and 21 cm high). To use another size, right-click the layout page and choose Page Properties…, or choose Layout ▸ Page Properties… in the menu. There you can choose from a list of standard paper sizes (A3, A5, Letter…), or enter a custom width and height.


Guides and helper grids

QGIS offers a few helper tools to finish the composition of your layout down to the last detail. Guides help you place items neatly on the layout page. You create vertical and horizontal guides in the Guides panel (J), or by dragging them from the ruler at the top or left of the layout page. For items to snap to these guides when you move them, make sure that View ▸ Snap to Guides is ticked.
A second tool is the helper grid, which you can enable with View ▸ Show Grid. In the Layout panel (H), under Guides and Grid, you set the spacing of this grid (H1). As with guides, QGIS can snap your items to this grid (View ▸ Snap to Grid).
In the Layout panel, under Guides and Grid, you can adjust the Snap tolerance (H2): how close an item has to come to a guide or grid line before it snaps.

title: 6.3 Composition and export
text:
Export formats
When your layout is ready, you can export it. In the Layout menu (A) or on the Layout toolbar, QGIS offers three export options:









Export as Image…
A raster image, for example PNG, JPG or TIFF.



Export as SVG…
A vector drawing that you can edit further in a drawing program.



Export as PDF…
A PDF document, for example to print or to share.



After choosing Export as Image…, you first choose a file name and the file format (for example PNG, JPG or TIFF). A second window then shows the resolution. QGIS fills it in from Export resolution in the Layout panel (H3), but you can still change it here. Choose the format and resolution with the use of your map in mind. TIFF files are suitable for printing, but usually too large for online use.






For printing, a minimum resolution of 300 dpi is often recommended. Keep in mind that a dpi value only makes sense in relation to the printed size: if the map is printed smaller or larger than your layout page, the effective resolution changes too. For a screen or a web page, file size usually matters more, so a lower resolution is often preferred.

title: 6.3 Composition and export
text:
Other tips
There are no fixed rules for the graphic design of a map: aesthetics is subjective, and good choices depend on the context. The recommendations below can still serve as general tips when you design your map.

Some more tips:

Print size: design your map at the size at which it will be published, because that determines the font size, the size of the symbols, the resolution (dpi)…
Colour: if your map will only be published in black and white, design it in black and white as well. That way you can judge whether the shades of grey are distinct enough.
Amount of information: avoid maps with too much information. Too much text or too many layers make a map unclear. Move information to the legend, or spread it over several maps.
Uniform positioning: use Position and Size and the guides to place all elements precisely and in line with each other.

title: 7.1.1 Working with GeoPackages
text:
On Common file formats in QGIS you learned what a GeoPackage is: a single database file that can hold several layers. This section shows how to use a GeoPackage in practice:
The image below shows where you find most of these options in QGIS. The letters are used in the text below.

title: 7.1.1 Working with GeoPackages
text:
Creating a GeoPackage
You already know how to save a layer as a GeoPackage. This is the default format in QGIS when creating a new vector layer. In fact, when you do this, you create not only a new layer but also an entirely new database that stores it.
You can also start with an empty GeoPackage database and add layers to it later. One way to do this is to right-click GeoPackage in the Browser panel (B) and choose Create Database….

title: 7.1.1 Working with GeoPackages
text:
Saving layers in a GeoPackage

New layers
You can add a new, empty layer to a GeoPackage with the New GeoPackage Layer button  on the Data Source Manager Toolbar (A) (or Layer ▸ Create Layer ▸ New GeoPackage Layer…). Next to File name, select your existing GeoPackage and give the layer a name under Table name. Then click OK and choose Add New Layer. You will learn how to fill a new empty layer from scratch in Manual vectorising.


Existing layers
There are several ways to save existing layers in a GeoPackage.

GeoPackage section in the Browser panel
The easiest method is to drag one or more layers onto your GeoPackage in the Browser panel (B). Alternatively, you can right-click your GeoPackage there and choose Import Vector Layer…. An import window will pop up where you can set the Table name, the Output CRS and the fields to include.


Save Features As…
Another option is to export an existing layer into a GeoPackage. Right-click it in the Layers panel (C) and choose Export ▸ Save Features As… (vector) or Export ▸ Save As… (raster). Pay attention: for rasters, GeoPackage is not the default export format.


Under Format, select GeoPackage.
Next to File name, click the … button and select your existing GeoPackage, or type a name for a new one.
Under Layer name, type a new name for this layer.
Click OK. QGIS adds the layer to the existing file. Only if a layer with the same name already exists in the file does QGIS ask what to do (for vector layers, the options are Overwrite File, Overwrite Layer or Append to Layer).








Be careful when choosing Overwrite File: QGIS deletes the entire GeoPackage, including all its layers, and creates a new one containing only the layer you are saving. Overwrite Layer, on the other hand, replaces only the layer with the same name. Append to Layer adds all features of the layer as new features. QGIS does not check whether they are already in the layer, so appending twice gives duplicates.





Package layers
With the processing tool Package layers, you can store one or more layers at once in a new or an existing GeoPackage, together with their active style. This tool only works for vector layers.

Load the layers into your project.
Open the Processing Toolbox (D) (Processing ▸ Toolbox) and choose Database ▸ Package layers (or type package in the search box).
Under Input layers, click the … button and select all the layers you want to store.
Leave Overwrite existing GeoPackage unticked if you want to add the layers to an existing GeoPackage. If a layer with the same name already exists, it will be replaced. If you do tick this option, QGIS first deletes the existing database, including all the layers it contains.
Leave Save layer styles into GeoPackage ticked to store the active style of each layer along with its data. Only the active style is packed, the others are not stored with it.
Under Destination GeoPackage, choose Save to File… and select a new or an existing GeoPackage.
Click Run.





Using the GeoPackage layers in your project
QGIS does not change your original layers. It only makes copies of them in GeoPackage format. If one of the originals was loaded in your QGIS project, it stays there. The copies are not loaded, unless Add saved file to map was ticked in the export window.
If you want to use your newly created GeoPackage layers in your project, you have to replace the originals:

Remove the original layers from the Layers panel and add the corresponding layers from the GeoPackage in the Browser panel (B).
Alternatively, right-click the original layer and choose Change Data Source… to point it to the corresponding layer in the GeoPackage. This preserves the layer’s style and other settings.

title: 7.1.1 Working with GeoPackages
text:
Storing styles in a GeoPackage
Normally, how a layer is styled is stored in your project file, not with the data itself. If you add a GeoPackage layer to another project, or send the GeoPackage to someone else, the layer appears with a random default style. You can avoid this by storing the style inside the GeoPackage.
For any layer in your GeoPackage, you can do this as follows (see also Saving and reusing styles):

Right-click the layer in the Layers panel and choose Styles ▸ Save Style….
Under Save style, choose In datasource database.
Give the style a name. Optionally, tick Use as default style for this layer if you want QGIS to use this style when the layer is imported. Then click OK.

You can save several styles for the same layer in your GeoPackage.

title: 7.1.1 Working with GeoPackages
section: Renaming and deleting layers in a GeoPackage
text:
Renaming and deleting layers in a GeoPackage
In the Browser panel (B), open the GeoPackage (small arrow in front of it) and right-click a layer. Under Manage, you find the options to rename and to delete the layer. You can rename fields there too: open the layer and its Fields, and right-click a field. 






A layer that you delete from a GeoPackage cannot be recovered, so be careful.

title: 7.2.1 Delimited text files (CSV)
text: Geographic information is not always available as a GIS file. It is often provided in the form of a table, such as an Excel spreadsheet containing place names and coordinates. This page explains how to load these tables into QGIS using delimited text files.

title: 7.2.1 Delimited text files (CSV)
section: What is a delimited text file?
text:
What is a delimited text file?
A delimited text file is a simple and widely used file format for storing tabular data. The principle is straightforward: each line in the file represents one table row, and the columns are separated by a specific character. This is usually a comma or a semicolon, but it can also be a tab, a space or another character.










The same table of battles of the American Revolutionary War, in Excel (left) and as a delimited text file in a text editor (right).
Popular programs for working with tabular data, such as MS Excel, can easily read and create such delimited text files. By default, however, Excel uses its own format. When saving a spreadsheet, you can choose a different file format from the Save as type list. To create a delimited text file, select CSV (comma-separated values). It is advisable to choose the UTF-8 version, CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited), as this is the default encoding in QGIS. This ensures that accents and other special characters (é, ë, ç, etc.) are preserved correctly.







Despite their name, CSV files do not always use a comma as the delimiter. In fact, if your computer’s regional settings are set to Belgium, the default delimiter is usually a semicolon. This is because Belgian settings use a comma as the decimal separator (51,05 rather than 51.05).









Although QGIS can also open Excel files directly, using a delimited text file is particularly useful when your table contains spatial information: QGIS can turn its coordinates into geometries straight away.

title: 7.2.1 Delimited text files (CSV)
text:
Importing delimited text files
To add a delimited text file in QGIS, open the Data Source Manager (menu Layer ▸ Data Source Manager, or Ctrl+L) on the Delimited Text tab. A large configuration window opens.

First, select the file you want to load (A). Next, indicate the delimiter (B). By default, CSV (comma separated values) is selected. If you select Custom delimiters, QGIS shows checkboxes for common alternatives (Semicolon, Tab, Space…). Simply select the delimiter your file uses. If it is not in the list, you can enter it yourself next to Others.
At the bottom, under Sample Data (E), you can preview how QGIS interprets your data with the current import settings. This preview is useful throughout the configuration process, as it shows whether the data are split into columns correctly.
The image below shows what happens when you choose the wrong delimiter. The comma has been selected, although the file uses semicolons. As a result, several fields end up in a single column. The decimal commas, on the other hand, split numbers across two columns.

Under Record and Fields Options (C), you specify various properties of the file you want to load. For example:

Are there any lines at the top of the file that should be skipped? If so, enter the number under Number of header lines to discard.
Does the first row contain column names?
Are decimal numbers written with a comma or a point? If they use a comma, tick Decimal separator is comma. In that case, the delimiter is usually a semicolon, as in our example.
Should spaces before and after text strings be removed? If so, tick Trim fields.
Do you want to remove empty fields?

It is best to go through the available checkboxes to make sure the import is correct. Here too, the Sample Data (E) section is very useful.






If you select Discard empty fields, empty fields are removed completely and all following fields in the row move one column to the left. As a result, they can end up under the wrong column name. In many cases, you therefore do not want to turn this on.



Under Geometry Definition (D) you describe the spatial component of your data.

If your file contains no coordinates and only attributes, choose No geometry (attribute only table).
If your file contains point coordinates and the X and Y values are stored in separate columns, choose Point coordinates. In our example, the X field is LONGITUDE and the Y field is LATITUDE. If the coordinates are written as degrees, minutes and seconds (DMS), tick DMS coordinates. Pay attention: if, as in our example, the coordinates are in degrees but written as decimal numbers, do not tick this box. For example, 51° 3’ 0’’ is a DMS coordinate, whereas 51.05° is not.
If the geometries in your text file are described using a Well known text notation (WKT), choose this option. WKT is a standard notation for describing vector geometries. It specifies the geometry type, followed by the coordinates in brackets. Some examples:
POINT (-71.06 42.36)
LINESTRING (-71.06 42.36, -74.01 40.71, -77.04 38.90)
POLYGON ((-109.05 41.00, -102.05 41.00, -102.05 37.00, -109.05 37.00, -109.05 41.00))
Set the Geometry CRS (if applicable): the coordinate reference system in which the coordinates in your file are written. If you choose the wrong CRS, your data end up in the wrong place. See Coordinate system of your geodata.







Try it yourself: From map to text



We already mentioned the Sample Data section (E). Don’t forget to check whether QGIS has detected the correct field type for each column. If not, adjust it in the drop-down list above the column.
Once you have configured all the settings, you can add the text file to your QGIS project.

title: 7.2.1 Delimited text files (CSV)
section: Converting a CSV file to a GeoPackage
text:
Converting a CSV file to a GeoPackage






CSV files offer far fewer possibilities in QGIS than GIS files such as GeoPackages or shapefiles. For example, you cannot simply edit the data from a CSV file. It is therefore usually a good idea to convert the imported CSV file to a GeoPackage.



How to do this is explained in Working with GeoPackages.
The list of battles was derived from Wikipedia, List of American Revolutionary War battles, October 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0).

title: 7.2.2 Web formats
text:
Some GIS formats are mainly used in a web context. They are not the first choice for working in QGIS, but QGIS can import and use them. This comes in handy because some data providers only offer their data in this way. Two of them are used particularly often: GeoJSON and KML. Both are text files describing geographic datasets using a certain syntax. Unlike CSV files, these are real GIS files: the geometry is already described in the file, so QGIS can show it on the map at once.
Another related format that you have probably heard of is GPX (GPS Exchange Format). It also describes geographic data, but it has a different purpose: exchanging GPS data between devices and apps.

title: 7.2.2 Web formats
7.2.2 Web formats
text:
GPX

Characteristics
GPX (.gpx) is meant for storing and exchanging GPS data: what a GPS device or app records or needs for navigation. It is not suitable for describing complex geographic features. A GPX file consists of three main elements:

waypoints (wpt): single points, for example the places you marked.
routes (rte): a planned route.
tracks (trk): the path that you covered and that was recorded by your GPS device.

Every point, including the points of routes and tracks, can also store an elevation and a time. Like KML, GPX is a text file in XML, with longitude and latitude in WGS 84.


In QGIS
QGIS opens a GPX file like any other vector file: drag it into the map canvas. QGIS first shows a list of the layers in the file, including the empty ones. Choose the ones you need. Waypoints are loaded as a point layer, routes and tracks as line layers.

title: 7.3.1 Services
text:
So far, you have always imported local files into QGIS: data that you had on your own computer. You often get such files as a download from a data provider, such as a government.
However, geodata (especially raster data) can be large files that you do not always want to store on your computer (imagine, for example, that you had to download the whole of Google Maps). Moreover, data providers are sometimes willing to make their information available for (restricted) use, but not for download. For these reasons, among others, it is sometimes useful or necessary to load data into your QGIS project from the servers of data providers. Technically, there are several services that make this possible, including:

WMS (Web Map Service)
WMTS (Web Map Tile Service)
XYZ Tile Service

As already mentioned in Data sources, you do not need to know exactly how these services work to use them well, but this is the main difference:
WMTS and XYZ services tend to be faster than WMS. They send tiles, small square pieces of the map that fit together and can be pre-rendered on the provider’s servers. A WMS, on the other hand, generates a new image each time you pan or zoom and sends this custom map to your computer. With all three, what you receive is an image (a raster), even if the server made it from vector data. You can look at it, but you cannot edit the features on it or use them in analyses.






Each zoom level of a tiled map has its own tiles, which can show different information: when you are zoomed out, you see only countries and major cities; when you zoom in, you see streets and buildings. The provider can pre-render all these tiles. When you look at a map, your computer only receives the tiles it needs for that zoom level and that area. Both make loading the map fast.



In fact, ‘loading’ data from external servers is not fundamentally different from importing local files. You already learned earlier that data are never stored in QGIS itself: when you import data, QGIS only creates a connection to the data source. In principle, it does not matter whether this source is on your computer or elsewhere. In practice, having your own copy often gives you more freedom, because data providers usually limit what you can do with their data.

title: 7.3.1 Services
text:
Example: XYZ Tiles
Several organisations have created base maps and provide access to them. Some of these are governments, others are commercial companies, such as Google or Esri. Others again are open, community-driven projects, such as OpenStreetMap: a detailed, up-to-date map of the world, created and maintained by volunteers.
Such base maps are usually provided via one of the services we discussed above. Creating a connection to them in QGIS is easy: all it takes is often just a URL. Data providers publish these URLs in their documentation. Take OpenStreetMap as an example. Its wiki has a list of raster tile providers, each with its own URL to make the connection:

Part of the table of base maps on the OpenStreetMap wiki page ‘Raster tile providers’ (consulted 16 October 2026; OpenStreetMap Wiki, CC BY-SA 2.0; map tiles © OpenStreetMap contributors). The red box shows the tile URL of the standard OpenStreetMap map.
In the documentation, you see that the tile URL of OpenStreetMap’s standard layer is:
https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png
The structure of the URL clearly shows that this is an XYZ service. To create such a connection in your QGIS window, right-click XYZ Tiles in the Browser panel, choose New Connection…, give the connection a name (e.g. OpenStreetMap), paste the URL you’ve found in the documentation and click OK.






{z} stands for the zoom level, {x} and {y} for the column and row of a tile. QGIS fills these in automatically.



Once you have created the connection, the layer becomes available under XYZ Tiles in the Browser panel. In the case of an XYZ service there is always just one layer, but other services can contain more. All you need to do is drag it into your project.










The OpenStreetMap layer is not stored in the software itself, nor is it on your computer: a connection is made to the data on the OpenStreetMap servers through the XYZ Tiles service. Background map © OpenStreetMap contributors.






Depending on the version and your settings, QGIS may already have a predefined connection to OpenStreetMap under XYZ Tiles in the Browser panel. This connection is no different from the one we made manually above.

title: 7.3.1 Services
text:
Example: WMS
For the second example, we use open data provided by the Flemish government. Its metadata catalogue lists, among others, hundreds of WMS, WMTS and WFS services. The record of each of these services gives its address.
We open the record of the service for historical cartography. The following link is listed as its WMS access point:
https://geo.api.vlaanderen.be/histcart/wms
To use it, right-click WMS/WMTS in the Browser panel, choose New Connection…, give the connection a name, paste the address and click OK.










Your Browser panel now shows a connection to the data on the server of the Flemish government. You can browse through several folders containing various layers with geographic information. Drag the layers you want to add into your project (or double-click them). 







QGIS remembers service connections for future projects. To remove a connection, right-click it in the Browser panel and choose Remove Connection….



The examples above show XYZ and WM(T)S services, but you create WFS, WCS and ArcGIS REST connections in a similar way. A WFS is different in one respect: you receive the features themselves, not an image.






You can now do Exercise 2.

title: 7.3.2 Databases
text:
You already know one kind of spatial database: the GeoPackage, a single file on your computer (see Working with GeoPackages). This page is about something else: database servers. The data are then not in a file that you open, but in a database system that runs as a separate program, usually on a server. To reach it, you need connection details.
Using databases has several advantages for data management. For example, it is much easier to work on the same dataset as a team. Moreover, the data are easier to use in a wide range of applications other than specialised GIS software. A database also makes it easier to integrate your geodata into a more advanced data model. On the other hand, setting up and maintaining a database system requires some technical knowledge.
There are several database systems that are suitable for processing geographic data, such as

PostgreSQL (with the PostGIS extension, which adds support for geographic data)
MS SQL (Structured Query Language) Server
Oracle
…

In QGIS you can easily connect to one of these systems through the Browser panel or the Data Source Manager. Although each database type has its own configuration window, the connection process is similar for all of them.

title: 7.3.2 Databases
text:
Connecting to PostgreSQL
As an example, we connect to a PostgreSQL database called USA. In the Browser panel, right-click PostgreSQL and choose New Connection….
A new window opens in which you have to enter some connection details, such as a name for the connection, the host, the port, the name of the database, your user name and your password… After you have filled in all the necessary details, click OK.










The connection now appears under PostgreSQL in the Browser panel. Open it to see the tables that contain geometries, and drag the ones you want into your project.

title: 7.4 Interactive
text: Try out what you learned in this chapter. Drag, click and change the settings as much as you like, you can’t break anything!

title: 7.4 Interactive
text:
From map to text
Draw points, lines or polygons on the map and see how they are written as text in GeoJSON, in KML and in a CSV file with WKT. You can download the result and open it in QGIS. A file can hold points, lines and polygons together, but a layer in QGIS holds only one geometry type:

GeoJSON and KML: QGIS asks which types you want to add and makes one layer per type.
CSV: choose WGS 84 as Geometry CRS and pick one Geometry type. QGIS loads only the features of that type, the rest are left out.

See the theory: Delimited text files and Web formats.

Open the tool full screen

title: Exercise 2: Transport in Belgium (1770–1880)
text:
Dataset: Transport in Belgium (1770–1880)
Around 1880, Belgium was one of the most industrialised countries in the world. In this exercise you map some of the infrastructure projects of that time: railways and stations, and the canals and docks that were built between 1770 and 1880. You then compare it with a 19th-century map that you load from the servers of the Flemish and the Walloon government. You practise importing data in several formats (Excel, CSV with coordinates and with WKT, GeoJSON, KML), saving them in a GeoPackage with their style, and connecting to WMS services.

title: Exercise 2: Transport in Belgium (1770–1880)
text:
Transport in Belgium around 1880
You can do this after chapter 7.

Add all vector data of the dataset to a new project and display them on the map canvas.
Make sure that only the railway stations opened between 1832 and 1880 are shown.
Save all data that are in a less suitable format in one GeoPackage, transport_1880.gpkg, together with the style you gave them.
Add the Vandermaelen map (1846–1854) as a background layer, for both Flanders and Wallonia.

title: Solution 2: Transport in Belgium (1770–1880)
text: This solution follows the steps of the exercise.

title: Solution 2: Transport in Belgium (1770–1880)
text:
Transport in Belgium around 1880

1. All vector data on the map
Railways. QGIS cannot read WKT from an Excel sheet. In Excel, choose File ▸ Save As with file type CSV UTF-8 and save the sheet as railways_1880.csv. Then open the Data Source Manager ▸ Delimited Text. WKT always uses a point as the decimal separator, whatever your settings.

Stations. The file uses a semicolon between the columns and a comma as the decimal separator. About 100 stations have no coordinates. They are in the attribute table, but not on the map.

Canals, docks and seaports. Drag waterways_1880.geojson into QGIS. The file holds lines (canals and docks) and points (the seaports), and a layer can only hold one geometry type. QGIS therefore asks which layers to add. Add both.

Rivers and Belgium. Drag navigable_rivers.kml and belgium.gpkg into QGIS. Show Belgium with an outline only (Simple Fill ▸ Fill style No Brush).
See Delimited text files (CSV) and Web formats.


2. Stations opened between 1832 and 1880
Choose a Graduated style on opened with 2 classes, and change the values of the classes by hand (double-click them). Untick the second class. QGIS has no separate manual mode: after you change the values by hand, Mode still shows the method you started from. Stations without a year in opened belong to no class and are not shown either: for those, the year is not known. See Graduated symbology.



3. Everything in one GeoPackage
The CSV files, the GeoJSON and the KML are good for exchanging data, but less suitable for working with them.

In the Browser panel, right-click GeoPackage ▸ Create Database… and create transport_1880.gpkg.
In the Processing Toolbox, open Database ▸ Package layers, select the five layers and the new GeoPackage, and click Run. Save layer styles into GeoPackage stores the style of each layer as well.
Replace the original layers in your project by the layers from the GeoPackage.


Other ways work as well, for example Export ▸ Save Features As… per layer, followed by Styles ▸ Save Style… ▸ In datasource database. See Working with GeoPackages.


4. Vandermaelen map for Flanders and Wallonia
The map exists as two services, one per region (see Services):

Flanders: search for Vandermaelen in the metadata catalogue of the Flemish government (https://metadata.vlaanderen.be). The record of the service for historical cartography gives the address https://geo.api.vlaanderen.be/histcart/wms. Add the layer Topografische kaart Vandermaelen (1846-1854), Vlaanderen.
Wallonia: search for Vandermaelen on the Géoportail de la Wallonie (https://geoportail.wallonie.be). The record of Cartes de Vandermaelen (1846-1854) gives the address https://geoservices.wallonie.be/arcgis/services/CARTES_ANCIENNES/VDML/MapServer/WMSServer.

For each, create a connection (Browser ▸ right-click WMS/WMTS ▸ New Connection…) and drag the map into your project, at the bottom of the Layers panel.

title: 8.1 Querying data: introduction
text: In the previous chapters you have already seen how to use GIS to visualise and store spatial information. You can go one step further and also query your data. You can do this on the basis of the attributes: in that case you can for example look for all features that have a certain field value in the attribute table. You can also query your data spatially. Then you can look among other things for features that lie within, near or next to other features.

title: 8.1 Querying data: introduction
text: In the previous chapters you have already seen how to use GIS to visualise and store spatial information. You can go one step further and also query your data. You can do this on the basis of the attributes: in that case you can for example look for all features that have a certain field value in the attribute table. You can also query your data spatially. Then you can look among other things for features that lie within, near or next to other features.

title: 8.1 Querying data: introduction
text:
Querying data in practice
In QGIS querying data can have different goals. The following pages cover them:

Selecting and extracting data: you select the features of a layer that meet certain conditions, or extract them straight into a new layer.
Filtering the attribute table: you only show the records that meet certain conditions.
Statistical queries: you calculate statistical values for your vector or raster data.

QGIS provides several querying tools with a configuration window: you simply click the settings you want. That makes them easy to use but also limits what you can ask. For more complex questions you can query your data with expressions. These are explained in chapter 9 Expressions.

title: 8.3 Filtering the attribute table
text: Another way to focus on specific features is to filter the contents of the attribute table. This lets you temporarily hide features that do not meet your criteria, without affecting their visibility in the map canvas.

title: 8.3 Filtering the attribute table
section: Filtering by selection, visibility and edit status
text:
Filtering by selection, visibility and edit status
By default the attribute table shows all features of your layer. Sometimes you only want to see the features that meet certain conditions. For this QGIS offers several filter methods. 
You will find the available filters in the drop-down menu at the bottom of the attribute table window.

Instead of all features (Show All Features) you can choose to show only the features that are selected (Show Selected Features) or that are located in the area visible in the map canvas (Show Features Visible On Map). If you choose Show Edited and New Features, only the records with unsaved changes will be shown.

title: 8.3 Filtering the attribute table
text:
Filtering by values
With Field Filter you filter on one field: choose the field in the submenu, type a value in the box that appears below the table and press Enter. For a text field QGIS shows all rows that contain this text. For a number field the value must match exactly.







At the top of the attribute table you can always see how many rows there are in total (Total) and how many are still shown after filtering (Filtered).



For more complex filters, on several fields or with spatial conditions, you use Advanced Filter (Expression). How to write such expressions is explained in chapter 9 Expressions.

title: 8.2.1 Selecting features
text:
Selecting features is a common task when working with vector layers in QGIS. By default selected features are highlighted in yellow in the map canvas and appear as blue rows in the attribute table.

Selections are useful for many purposes, from highlighting specific features to using them as input for further operations. This page and the next explain how selections work, what they are used for and how to create them.

title: 8.2.1 Selecting features
text:
Selecting features is a common task when working with vector layers in QGIS. By default selected features are highlighted in yellow in the map canvas and appear as blue rows in the attribute table.

Selections are useful for many purposes, from highlighting specific features to using them as input for further operations. This page and the next explain how selections work, what they are used for and how to create them.

title: 8.2.1 Selecting features
text:
Why select features?
You can use a selection to:

Highlighting specific features: a selection makes certain features stand out on the map, which can be useful during data exploration and analysis.
Navigating to selected features: the map canvas can be centred on the selection using Pan Map to Selection , or zoomed in using Zoom to Selection . 
Using selected features in tools: many QGIS tools can work on a selection instead of processing the entire layer. In most Processing tools this is controlled by the Selected features only checkbox under the input layer.
Copying features to another layer: selected features can be copied with Edit ▸ Copy Features and pasted into another layer of the same geometry type (points, lines or polygons) with Edit ▸ Paste Features. That layer must be in edit mode. With Edit ▸ Paste Features As the copied features go to a new layer instead.
Saving a selection as a separate layer: a selection can be exported as a new vector layer, which makes it permanent. This is useful for example to create a compact dataset with only the features you need. Loading large datasets can slow QGIS down.
To do this, right-click the relevant layer in the Layers panel and choose Export ▸ Save Selected Features As…. In the Save Vector Layer as… dialog, Save only selected features is already enabled.
The same dialog opens through Export ▸ Save Features As…, but in this case the Save only selected features option must be ticked manually.
You can also use the Processing tool Extract selected features (in the Processing Toolbox under Vector general). It copies the selected features to a new layer, either a temporary layer or a file.








Selections are volatile: they are only temporarily marked in a project session and not stored anywhere. Once they are gone, there is no way to retrieve them.

title: 8.2.2 Automated selections & extractions
text:
You can make ad hoc selections both in your map canvas and in your attribute table, simply by clicking the features you want. You already learned this in Navigating the map canvas and The attribute table.
The tools for automated selections are in the Processing Toolbox, under Vector selection. Each Select by … tool there has an Extract by … variant, which puts the matching features in a new layer instead of selecting them.

title: 8.2.2 Automated selections & extractions
text:
Based on attribute value
When you need to select or extract many features that share a particular attribute value, selecting them one by one is slow and error-prone. QGIS can do this automatically using the Select by attribute or Extract by attribute tool. Double-click it in the Processing Toolbox to open it.
In the configuration window, specify:

Input layer: the layer you want to select features from.
Selection attribute: the attribute field you want to use.
Operator: the condition the value must meet, such as =, > or is not null.
Value: the value you want to compare the field against.
Modify current selection by: what happens to any existing selection. You can create a new selection, add the matching features to the current one, select within it or remove from it.











In the example above we select all US states that had joined the United States by the end of the Civil War. Choose the states layer and the field STATEHOOD, which contains the year in which each state joined. Then choose the operator ≤ and the value 1865. Click Run to make the selection.

title: 8.2.2 Automated selections & extractions
text:
Based on location
Besides attribute values, the position of features can also be a criterion: do they overlap, cross or touch features in another layer? For such spatial relationships, use Select by location or Extract by location, which you open in the same way.
In the configuration window, specify:

Select features from: the layer you want to select features from.
Where the features (geometric predicate): the spatial relationship, for example are within or intersect. You can choose multiple predicates at once. A feature is then selected as soon as it meets one of them.
By comparing to the features from: the reference layer.
Modify current selection by: what happens to any existing selection, as in Select by attribute.











The example above shows how to find the battles of the American Civil War that were not fought on land. Choose the civil_war_battles layer, the predicate disjoint (no point in common) and the reference layer states, and click Run. You will notice that most of the selected points indeed lie in harbours, bays and sounds along the coast, for example at Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor.






Try it yourself: see what the other predicates do in Select by location.



One setting we have not discussed yet is the Selected features only checkbox. When you tick it, QGIS only takes the selected features of the reference layer into account.










This time the question is which Civil War battles were fought in Kentucky. First select Kentucky by hand in the states layer. Then open Select by location again: select features from civil_war_battles, with the predicate are within and states as the reference layer, and tick Selected features only. QGIS now only selects the battles in Kentucky. Without the checkbox, it would select the battles that were fought in any state.






Some questions need more than one attribute value or one spatial relation. For those you can select with an expression. You will learn how in chapter 9 Expressions.



* In the maps on this page, the selected points have a black outline for clarity. You can change the look of selected features in Layer Properties ▸ Rendering ▸ Selections ▸ Override symbol for selected features.

title: 8.4.1 Statistics of vector data
text: So far you have explored different ways to query geodata and focus on specific features. You can also query your data through statistical analysis. Rather than identifying specific features, statistical tools help you summarise and analyse data by calculating statistical values for an entire dataset or for groups of features. This page introduces statistical tools for vector data.

title: 8.4.1 Statistics of vector data
text:
Querying attribute data statistically

Basic statistics for fields
The Basic statistics for fields tool lets you quickly calculate simple statistical values (such as mean, median, minimum, maximum, quantiles…) for a specific attribute field of a vector layer.
You open it via Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector analysis ▸ Basic statistics for fields. In the tool window, choose the layer and the field you want to analyse statistically, and click Run.










You do not see the result of the calculations immediately. Instead, a new link appears in the Results Viewer panel. Double-click it to open the report:






Statistics by categories
The Statistics by categories tool calculates statistics for groups of features. It uses the values in an attribute field to divide the features into categories.
For example, you have a point layer containing the major cities of the United States. Its attribute table includes fields with their population and the state they belong to. You can use Statistics by categories to group the cities by state and calculate population statistics for each group. In the tool window, configure the following parameters:

Input vector layer: select the layer you want to analyse (major_cities).
Field to calculate statistics on: select the field containing the values you want to analyse (POPULATION).
Field(s) with categories: select the field QGIS should use to group the features (STATE_ABBR).











The tool creates a new table with the statistics, one row per state. You can open this table via the Layers panel.

In the row of Texas, for example, you can read that the layer contains 263 Texan cities (count) with 19 772 314 inhabitants in total (sum), and that the largest has 2 304 580 inhabitants (max).

title: 8.4.1 Statistics of vector data
text:
Querying geometries statistically
You can calculate statistics not only for attribute fields, but also for your geometries. Below are a few of the options, all in the Processing Toolbox.

You can apply Vector analysis ▸ Nearest neighbour analysis to a vector layer with point geometries. Among other things, it calculates the mean distance from each point to its nearest neighbouring point.
You can apply Vector analysis ▸ Overlap analysis to a polygon layer. For each polygon, it calculates how much of its area overlaps with another layer, as an area and as a percentage.
You can apply Vector general ▸ Join attributes by location (summary) to two layers. It calculates statistics for the features of one layer that overlap with the features of another layer, and writes them to a new layer. Chapter 12 comes back to this tool.

For example, for the Civil War battles (in EPSG:5070, a CRS in metres), Nearest neighbour analysis gives a mean distance of about 47 km to the nearest other battle. On the map, each black line connects a battle with the nearest other battle:










You can now do Exercise 3, part A.

title: 8.4.2 Statistics of raster data
text: You can also query raster data statistically. The Processing Toolbox provides several tools for this purpose under Raster analysis.

title: 8.4.2 Statistics of raster data
text:
Raster layer statistics
Raster layer statistics calculates basic statistical values for a raster band, such as the mean, the minimum and maximum value, and the standard deviation. Open Processing Toolbox ▸ Raster analysis ▸ Raster layer statistics to use it.
In the tool window, choose the layer and the Band number you want to analyse statistically, and click Run.










As with Basic statistics for fields on the previous page, the result appears as a link in the Results Viewer panel. Double-click it to open the report:

title: 8.4.2 Statistics of raster data
text:
Raster minimum/maximum
Raster minimum/maximum finds the lowest and highest cell values in a raster band. The output is a vector layer containing two points: one at the centre of a cell with the lowest value and one at the centre of a cell with the highest value.
Applied to a raster layer with the average global temperatures in August, the tool finds the warmest cell in the Sahara (38.4 °C) and the coldest near the South Pole (−66.5 °C):

title: 8.4.2 Statistics of raster data
text:
Raster layer unique values report
Raster layer unique values report lists all unique cell values in a raster band. For each value, it shows the number of cells and their total area. You have already used this tool in Report of unique cell values in chapter 4.

title: 8.4.2 Statistics of raster data
text:
Zonal statistics
Zonal statistics calculates statistics for the raster cells that overlap with each polygon of a vector layer. You will learn more about this tool in chapter 13.

title: 8.5 Interactive
text: Try out what you learned in this chapter. Drag, click and change the settings as much as you like, you can’t break anything!

title: 8.5 Interactive
text:
Select by location
Drag an area across a map of the United States and see which cities, rivers or states are selected with each spatial relation. Click a feature to see which relations are true for it. See the theory: Based on location.

Open the tool full screen

From about 1200, beguinage courts were founded in the Low Countries: communities of beguines, religious women who lived together without taking permanent vows. title: Solution 3: Beguinages in the Low Countries
section: Part A: Highlighting and extracting beguinage courts
text:
Part A: Highlighting and extracting beguinage courts

1. Layers in Belgian Lambert 72
Drag beguinages.gpkg into QGIS and add all five layers. The data are in ETRS89-LAEA (EPSG:3035), a coordinate system for the whole of Europe. For Belgium, Belgian Lambert 72 (EPSG:31370) is a good choice (see Projected coordinate systems).
Set the project to EPSG:31370 (bottom right in the status bar). To convert the layers themselves, open Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector general ▸ Reproject layer for each layer, choose EPSG:31370 as Target CRS and save the result in a new GeoPackage. With Run as Batch Process… you convert all five layers at once. Export ▸ Save Features As… works as well.



2. Dedicated to the Virgin Mary
Many beguinage courts are dedicated to more than one saint, for example “Virgin Mary / St. Agnes / St. Catherine”. Open Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector selection ▸ Select by attribute on beguinages and choose the field dedication, the operator contains and the value Virgin Mary (see Automated selections). Contains also finds these combinations. Search for the full name “Virgin Mary”, so that Mary Magdalen is left out. Upper and lower case count: type Virgin Mary exactly like this.

After chapter 9 you can also select them with an expression in Select Features by Expression (see Text fields). % stands for any number of characters:
"dedication" LIKE '%Virgin Mary%'

10 beguinage courts are dedicated (also) to the Virgin Mary, among them “St. John and Virgin Mary” and “Consolation of Virgin Mary”. One of them, “Virgin Mary / St. Mary Magdalen”, is dedicated to both.


3. Founded before 1250, outside present-day Belgium
First open Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector selection ▸ Select by attribute on beguinages: field founded, operator <, value 1250. 29 beguinage courts are selected.
Then open Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector selection ▸ Select by location: select features from beguinages that are disjoint from the features from belgium, and under Modify current selection by choose selecting within current selection (see Automated selections).

9 of the 29 early beguinage courts lie outside present-day Belgium: Aachen (Saint Matthias), Aardenburg, Cambrai, Douai, Hesdin, Le Quesnoy, Lille, Middelburg and Valenciennes.


4. UNESCO World Heritage
Open Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector selection ▸ Extract by attribute on beguinages: field unesco, operator =, value 1. unesco is a Boolean field: in this tool you type TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0. With the value true the tool finds nothing. Save Extracted (attribute) as for example beguinages_unesco (13 beguinage courts) and Extracted (non-matching) as beguinages_other (75): one run gives you both layers.

Then open Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector analysis ▸ Basic statistics for fields on the fields founded and closed of each new layer (see Statistical queries). The statistics of closed, for the UNESCO beguinage courts (left) and the others (right):

The founding years hardly differ: the beguinage courts on the UNESCO list are not much older than the others. The closing years differ a lot. All of them existed until the second half of the 19th century or later, and three still exist (their closing year is empty). They are on the list because they survived, not because they were the first.

title: Solution 3: Beguinages in the Low Countries
text:
Part B: Calculating new information

1. Lifespan
Open the Field Calculator on beguinages, create a new field lifespan of type Integer (32 bit) and subtract the two years (see The Field Calculator):
"closed" - "founded"

For the beguinage courts that still exist, the closing year is empty, so the result is NULL. Select them with Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector selection ▸ Select by attribute: field existing, operator =, value 1 (see Automated selections). Open the Field Calculator again, tick Only update … selected features, choose Update existing field lifespan, and subtract the founding year from the current year. You can type the current year yourself, or use year(now()): then the lifespan stays up to date.
year(now()) - "founded"



2. Area of the dioceses
Open the Field Calculator on dioceses, create a new field area_km2 of type Decimal number (real) and use $area / 1000000 (see The Field Calculator).

$area calculates the area on the ellipsoid of the project, in m², so the result is reliable for dioceses far from Belgium too. QGIS can only do this correctly when the layer has the right CRS: after task A1, all layers are in Belgian Lambert 72. Check the ellipsoid in Project ▸ Properties ▸ General under Measurements (see Units of measurement).


3. Statistics per archdiocese
Open Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector analysis ▸ Statistics by categories, with dioceses as input layer, area_km2 as the field to calculate statistics on and archdiocese as the field with categories (see Statistical queries).

The new table has one row per ecclesiastical province. The row of Reims shows 12 dioceses with a mean area of about 4 770 km².



4. Distance to the nearest beguinage court
Open Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector analysis ▸ Nearest neighbour analysis on beguinages (see Statistical queries). The tool measures, for each beguinage court, the distance to the nearest other one, and gives the mean of these distances. The layer must be in a CRS in metres, which it is after task A1. The Observed mean distance is about 13 400 m: on average, the nearest other beguinage court lay about 13 km away, a few hours on foot.



5. Beguinage courts in the ecclesiastical province of Reims
First select the dioceses of the ecclesiastical province of Reims, for example with Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector selection ▸ Select by attribute on dioceses: field archdiocese, operator =, value Reims (12 dioceses). Then open Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector selection ▸ Extract by location: extract features from beguinages that are within the features from dioceses, with Selected features only ticked (see Automated selections). Save the result as beguinages_reims. It contains 46 beguinage courts.

Extract by location makes the new layer in one step. With Select by location, you first select the beguinage courts and then save them with Export ▸ Save Selected Features As….


6. Distance to the archbishop of Reims
Open the Field Calculator on beguinages_reims and create a new field dist_reims of type Decimal number (real). get_feature fetches the seat of Reims from the layer seats, and distance measures the distance in metres (see Retrieving features):
distance(@geometry, geometry(get_feature('seats', 'name', 'Reims'))) / 1000

Sort the attribute table on dist_reims: the nearest beguinage court is Avesnes-sur-Helpe, at about 105 km from Reims.
In task 4, the mean distance from a beguinage court to the nearest other beguinage court was about 13 km. The beguinage court nearest to Reims lies eight times as far from the seat of the archbishop. The beguinage courts lie close to each other, in the towns of Flanders, Hainaut and Brabant, but far from Reims.

section: Part C: Mapping the dioceses and the beguinage courts

Part C: Mapping the dioceses and the beguinage courts

1. Seats of bishops and archbishops
In the Layer Properties of seats, choose Categorized on type and click Classify. Double-click each symbol to give it its own shape and size (Simple Marker ▸ Shape, Size): in the map below a large black star for archdiocese and a small square for diocese. See Categorized symbology.



2. Diocese names with rule-based labels
On the Labels tab of dioceses, choose Rule-based Labeling and add two rules (see Rules). The archdioceses are the dioceses whose name is the same as the value in archdiocese: Canterbury, Cologne, Mainz, Reims, Rouen and Trier.

Archdiocese: rule "name" = "archdiocese", value upper("name") (capitals), bold, a little larger.
Diocese: Else rule, value "name", italic.




3. How certain are the data?
In the Layer Properties of beguinages, choose Rule-based with three rules (see Rules):

Exact years (green dot): "founded_accuracy" = 'exact' AND "closed_accuracy" = 'exact'
Other (orange dot): NOT ("founded_accuracy" = 'exact' AND "closed_accuracy" = 'exact') OR "closed_accuracy" IS NULL
Location not certain (an exclamation mark): "position" = 'approximate'. For the symbol, choose the symbol layer type Font Marker and type !.


Keep the exclamation mark rule last, so that it lies on top of the dot. The rule for the orange dots is the opposite of the green rule, so that every beguinage court gets a dot, also when the exclamation mark rule applies to it. The beguinage courts that still exist have no closing year, so closed_accuracy is empty. For them the comparison gives NULL, and NOT NULL stays NULL (see NULL values). Without OR "closed_accuracy" IS NULL three beguinage courts would get no dot at all: Ghent (Our-Lady Ter Hooyen), Kortrijk and Sint-Amandsberg.
27 beguinage courts have an exact founding year and an exact closing year. 12 have a location that is not certain.


4. More than 500 years
Add a fourth rule to the rules of task 3: More than 500 years, "lifespan" > 500, with a dot of the same size, without fill and with a red outline. Put it below the green and orange rules, so that the red circle lies on top of the dot, and above the exclamation mark rule.

A beguinage court that meets several rules gets all their symbols. 42 beguinage courts existed for more than 500 years.

title: Solution 4: Historical city plans of Ghent
section: Part A: Gérard, a mid-19th-century parcel map
text:
Part A: Gérard, a mid-19th-century parcel map

1. Georeferencing the map sheets
Add OpenStreetMap via XYZ Tiles in the Browser panel (see Services), open Layer ▸ Georeferencer… and add one sheet with Open Raster. Add points on corners of buildings and street crossings that still exist, spread over the whole sheet.
Then open Settings ▸ Transformation Settings… (see Setting up the transformation):

Transformation type: the sheets are rotated (the top of each sheet points to the west), so Linear is unsuitable: it cannot rotate. Gérard’s map is accurate, so choose a transformation that distorts little: Helmert moves, rotates and scales the sheet, but keeps its shape (see Transformation types).
Target CRS: Belgian Lambert 72 (EPSG:31370), a projected CRS in metres made for Belgium.
Output file: a new GeoTIFF for each sheet. The scan itself stays unchanged.
Save GCP points: ticked, so that you can open and adjust the points again later.
Load in project when done: ticked, so that you see the result over OpenStreetMap.


Set the Transformation Settings as soon as you have the first few points: 2 for Helmert, 3 for Polynomial 1. From then on, QGIS can calculate where a place on the sheet lies on the reference map. Switch on the two link buttons, Link Georeferencer to QGIS and Link QGIS to Georeferencer (see The Georeferencer window): when you zoom or pan in one window, the other follows to the same place. This makes finding the next points a lot faster.
Click Start Georeferencing, and do the same for the other sheets.



2. The residuals
Each GCP has a residual: the distance between its target and the place where the transformation puts it. QGIS shows them in the GCP table, and their mean as Mean error in the status bar of the Georeferencer: the mean residual error. With well-placed points, the mean residual error for Gérard’s map comes down to a few metres at most on the ground. For Van Deventer’s map in chapter 10, it is larger. Gérard’s map is a parcel map based on the cadastral plans: it was surveyed and drawn to scale. Van Deventer drew his plan from his own measurements in the 16th century.


3. Other transformation types
Residuals measure the fit at the GCPs, not the overall positional accuracy of the georeferenced map. A smaller mean residual error therefore does not show which result is best. Polynomial 1 gives a smaller mean residual error than Helmert because it may do more to reach the GCPs: it can also scale the sheet a little differently in the two directions and skew it. Polynomial 2 and Thin Plate Spline go further still: they bend the map. With Thin Plate Spline, every GCP is matched exactly to its target, so the residuals at the GCPs are zero, regardless of whether the points were placed accurately. However, incorrectly placed GCPs can cause severe distortions in the resulting map.
A transformation that distorts little can be an advantage. Small inaccuracies in the placement of GCPs or in the original map are not forced to fit exactly. Instead, the transformation finds the parameters that minimise the sum of squared residuals across all GCPs. As a result, small errors can partly compensate for each other. For an accurate map like Gérard’s, Helmert or Polynomial 1 keeps the map as it was drawn.

title: Solution 4: Historical city plans of Ghent
section: Part B: de Wit, an engraving from a town atlas (end of the 17th century)
text:
Part B: de Wit, an engraving from a town atlas (end of the 17th century)

1. Georeferencing on OpenStreetMap
Repeat the procedure of Part A. Here too, find homologous points and choose a transformation type that suits the map and your aim. For this plan, the choice of transformation type can turn out differently, depending on the final aim of the georeferencing. If the plan should stay visually attractive, for example to show it as a whole over a modern map, Helmert keeps it as it was drawn. If you want to match individual streets or buildings as closely as possible, Thin Plate Spline may be a better choice, provided that you use many carefully placed and well-distributed GCPs. Each choice has its drawbacks. With Helmert, the local errors of the plan remain. With Thin Plate Spline, straight streets and walls can become curved between the points, and a badly placed point pulls the plan out of shape around it.

The mean residual error is clearly larger than for Gérard’s map. The plan contains pictorial elements drawn in bird’s-eye view: buildings are shown in perspective, so it is sometimes difficult to determine the exact ground position of towers and other prominent structures. Points on the ground work best, such as squares, bridges and corners of the fortifications. However, suitable control points are not always available, so you sometimes have to rely on the corresponding points that you can identify with confidence.



2. The Ferraris map as base map
Add the Ferraris map via the WMS (Browser ▸ right-click WMS/WMTS ▸ New Connection…) and use it instead of OpenStreetMap when you choose the target points.

Advantage: more corresponding features can be identified on both maps. Town gates, the fortifications, the Spanish Castle and many streets of de Wit’s plan still existed in 1777, but have disappeared or changed since.
Disadvantage: the Ferraris map is not geometrically perfect either: it contains its own positional errors and distortions. When you use it as the reference, these errors are transferred to the georeferenced de Wit map. The accuracy of your result is therefore limited by the accuracy of the reference map as well as by the accuracy of the original plan.

Vectorising the castle
You can do this after chapter 11.

Add the Ferraris map to a new project and zoom in to the Spanish Castle. Create a new GeoPackage named spanish_castle.gpkg containing five layers: pois (points, with a text field named description), walls (lines), and moat, castle_grounds and buildings (polygons).
Digitise the area enclosed by the castle walls as a single polygon in the castle_grounds layer.
Digitise the windmill and the castle gate as point features in the pois layer. Make sure that the gate point lies exactly on the boundary of castle_grounds. Enter a description for each point.

Digitise the buildings inside the castle walls in the buildings layer. Adjacent buildings must share their boundaries, without gaps or overlaps. Represent courtyards enclosed by a building as holes in the corresponding polygon.

The Ferraris map shows the castle in detail: the moat, the walls and the buildings inside.


1. The Ferraris map and a GeoPackage with five layers
Create a connection to the WMS of the Flemish government (Browser ▸ right-click WMS/WMTS ▸ New Connection…, URL https://geo.api.vlaanderen.be/histcart/wms) and add the layer Ferrariskaart (1777), Vlaanderen (see Services). Switch on Enable Tracing. On walls, click a point on the edge of castle_grounds, then a second point further along it: tracing follows the edge between the two points. Close the line on its first point.

A new building is then cut off where it would overlap a building you drew before, so buildings that stand against each other share their walls. The buildings may overlap the grounds: they lie on top of them. For a courtyard, draw the building first, then cut the courtyard out with Add Ring (see Advanced digitizing).

title: 7.1.2 Editing the attribute table
text: In The attribute table you learned how to view attribute data. Often you need to do more than just consult them: you may want to change individual values, add or delete fields (columns), or update many values at once. QGIS provides tools for all of these tasks.

title: 7.1.2 Editing the attribute table
text:
Editing the attribute table

When you open the attribute table, you will notice that you cannot edit individual cells straight away. First you need to activate editing mode with Toggle editing mode  (A1).

Features
Once editing mode is active, you can edit individual cell values directly in the table: just click the cell you want to update and overwrite its content. Remember that each field has a type. You cannot enter text in a number field, for example.
You can also add, delete or copy whole features (rows). The buttons for this are grouped above the table (A5): Add feature via attribute table , Delete selected features , Cut selected rows to clipboard , Copy selected rows to clipboard  and Paste features from clipboard . The usual keyboard shortcuts work as well: Ctrl+X (cut), Ctrl+C (copy), Ctrl+V (paste) and Delete.
If you want to edit several features at once, you can use multi edit mode. Suppose you add a new field RESULT to the layer civil_war_battles and want to fill in Union victory for a few clear Union victories, such as the battles of Gettysburg, Fort Donelson and Five Forks:

Select the features you want to update (here these three battles).
Click Toggle multi edit mode  (A2). You can still adapt your selection in the list on the left.
Enter the new value in the box of the right field (here Union victory in RESULT). The icon next to it turns red.
Click apply changes in the yellow bar at the top of the form.


QGIS applies the values you entered to all selected features.


Attribute fields
Besides values and features, you can also add or delete attribute fields: with New field  (A7) and Delete field  (A8).

When adding a field, you need to specify its properties in the Add Field window:

Name: the name of the new field. In a shapefile, field names are limited to 10 characters. GeoPackages allow longer names.
Type: the type of data the field will contain, such as text, integer or decimal number.
Length: the maximum number of characters or digits the field can store.
Precision: for decimal fields, the number of digits after the decimal point.

Remember that the precision is included in the total field length. For example, if you set Length to 4 and Precision to 3, the field can store one digit before and three digits after the decimal point.






Once you have created a column, you cannot simply change the field type or the length. So always think carefully before you create a field!





Reloading data
If other users or programs edit the same data source at the same time, Reload the table  (A4) shows the latest version.

title: 7.1.2 Editing the attribute table
text:
Saving your edits
Always remember to save your edits with Save edits  (A3). Saving the project is not enough: as you learned in QGIS project, a project only stores a link to its data sources, not the data themselves. If you have edited several layers, save each of them separately. Otherwise your edits can be lost.

title: 7.1.2 Editing the attribute table
text:
Managing field structure
In the attribute table itself, you cannot change the name or the type of an existing field. Via a detour, though, you can achieve both.
You can rename an existing field in the Layer Properties. Open the Fields tab, activate editing mode and double-click the field name.
Changing a field’s type or length is in principle impossible. You can, however, create a copy of your layer with adjusted settings for specific attribute fields. For this you use the Refactor fields tool, which you find in the Processing Toolbox under Vector table. Its window lists all attribute fields of the layer with their current settings. Adjust the settings you want to change and click Run. The tool leaves the original layer unchanged and creates a new layer with the adjusted fields. This new layer is a full copy: it contains all features of the original layer, with their geometries and attribute values.






Because the data are copied as well, every existing value must fit the new field type. A text field that only contains numbers, such as 31, can become a number field. A text field with names, such as Nebraska, cannot. So make sure you clean or empty the fields you want to change before you use the tool.













As with other Processing tools, Refactor fields creates a temporary layer by default. If you want to keep working with it, save it as a permanent file, for example a GeoPackage layer (Save to GeoPackage… under Refactored).

title: 9.1 Expressions in QGIS
text:
QGIS has a very well-developed graphical user interface: it translates complex functionality into simple menus and configuration windows. Because of this, you can carry out many operations without understanding the processes behind them. However, these interfaces sometimes limit what you can do. Some operations require several steps or a lot of manual work. You have already encountered examples of this in earlier chapters:

Editing: In the attribute table, you can change values one by one or give several features the same value at once. However, you cannot do calculations, such as adding or subtracting the values of two existing fields.
Querying: Select by attribute or the attribute table filter check one condition at a time. You cannot combine conditions on several fields in one step.
Visualising: A style per category or a graduated style is based on a single field. You cannot easily define a feature’s symbol based on a combination of conditions.
Labelling: Single Labels show the value of one field, in the same style for every feature. You cannot vary the label or its style from one feature to another.

This is where expressions come in. They allow you to define more precisely what you want QGIS to do.

title: 9.1 Expressions in QGIS
text:
What?
Expressions are formulas that follow certain syntax rules. They are built from fields, values, operators (such as > or AND), functions and variables. Functions are predefined commands that perform a specific task. For example, area() calculates the area of a geometry, while upper() converts text to uppercase. Variables provide information about the current feature, layer or project. Examples include a feature’s geometry and the name of the current layer.
A very simple example of an expression in QGIS is:

When you apply an expression to a layer, for example to select features, QGIS evaluates the expression for each feature, one by one. In this example, it checks whether the value in the POPULATION field is greater than 1000000. If the condition is true, the feature is selected. If not, it is not selected.

title: 9.2.1 Querying
text:
Writing expressions can be challenging for new GIS users. Fortunately, QGIS provides a helpful tool: the Expression Builder.
In Processing tools such as Select by expression and Extract by expression (Processing Toolbox ▸ Vector selection), you can open the Expression Builder by clicking the epsilon button  next to the expression field.
You can also open the Expression Builder when filtering features in the attribute table. To do so, select Advanced Filter (Expression) at the bottom of the table.










The Expression Builder opens in a new window. It consists of four parts:


On the left (A), you write the expression itself. This expression must follow certain syntax rules so that QGIS can process it. You learn these rules on the following pages.
In the centre (B), you find an expandable list of fields and values, operators, functions and variables. You can use the search bar at the top of this list to find an option more quickly. If you double-click an option, it is inserted into the expression on the left (A). This helps you avoid typing errors.
On the right (C), you find the documentation of the option you selected in B.
At the bottom left (D), in the Preview section, QGIS shows the result of the expression for the first feature of the layer. You can use the arrow buttons to see the result for the next or previous feature, or choose another feature from the drop-down list. This allows you to check immediately whether your expression gives the expected output. If the expression is a comparison, the preview shows 1 (TRUE) or 0 (FALSE). If the expression contains an error, the preview shows Expression is invalid. Click (more info) to see what went wrong.
