title: 9.2.1 Querying
text:
Writing expressions as comparisons
When you use expressions to query your data, the expression usually takes the form of a comparison. A comparison checks two values, for example a field value and a number. If the comparison is TRUE for a feature, that feature is included in the result. If it is FALSE, the feature is not included.
For example, "POPULATION" > 1000000 checks whether each city has more than 1 000 000 inhabitants. Only the cities that meet this condition are included in the result.
Common comparison operators are =, <> (not equal to), >, >=, < and <=.

title: 9.2.2 Calculating
text: You can use expressions for more than querying your data. They can also perform calculations. This is particularly useful in the attribute table, where you can use expressions to calculate or update field values automatically.

title: 9.2.2 Calculating
text:
The Field Calculator
To perform these calculations, QGIS provides a tool: the Field Calculator. It looks and works almost the same way as the Expression Builder. The main difference is that it includes a few additional settings to control whether you want to create a new field or update an existing one.
Open the attribute table of the layer and click Open field calculator .

The Field Calculator opens in a new window. Here, you specify three things:


At the top (A), you choose which features to update: all features or only the selected ones. The option Only update … selected features is available only when features are selected.
Below it (B), you choose where to store the results: in a new attribute field (Create a new field) or in an existing field (Update existing field), which replaces the existing values.
At the bottom (C), you write the expression that calculates a value for each feature. This part looks and works exactly like the Expression Builder.

title: 9.2.2 Calculating
text:
Writing expressions as calculations
In the Field Calculator, expressions are generally used to calculate a value that you want to store in an attribute table. This can be the result of a mathematical operation, a text manipulation, or another type of calculation.
For example, "POP2010" - "POP1990" calculates the population increase between 1990 and 2010 for each feature. The resulting value is then written to the attribute table.
You can also use comparisons in the Field Calculator. In that case, the result is a Boolean value: 1 (TRUE) if the comparison is true, and 0 (FALSE) if it is not.






For raster layers, the Raster Calculator works in a similar way: it calculates a new value for every cell, with its own, simpler expressions. You will use it in chapter 13.

title: 9.3.1 Numeric fields
text: On this page we illustrate the use of numeric attribute fields in expressions with a few simple examples.

title: 9.3.1 Numeric fields
text:
Querying
Earlier in this chapter you already saw the expression "POPULATION" > 1000000. Here we show step by step how you build it. You have a layer with the major cities of the United States (major_cities), and you want to select the cities with more than 1 000 000 inhabitants. The number of inhabitants is in the field POPULATION, so you will have to use this field in your expression.










When you open the Expression Builder, you will find an overview of all available attribute fields under Fields and Values (B). If you insert the field POPULATION by double-clicking it, note that it is written between double quotation marks: "POPULATION". The double quotation marks tell QGIS that POPULATION is a field name. In certain cases QGIS recognises field names without them, but it is good practice to always use double quotation marks.
We want to test for each feature whether the number of inhabitants is greater than 1 000 000. Under Operators (B) you can find and double-click the greater-than sign. Then complete the expression yourself so that you get "POPULATION" > 1000000.
This expression is evaluated for every feature in the layer. Each time "POPULATION" is replaced with the actual value that the feature has in that field. For Chicago, the expression therefore becomes 2746388 > 1000000. The result is 1 (= TRUE). For Alabaster, on the other hand, it becomes 33284 > 1000000. The result is 0 (= FALSE), as you can also see in the preview above (D).
When you then click Select Features, only the features for which the result of the expression is 1 are selected. In the result below you can see that they all do indeed have more than 1 000 000 inhabitants.

title: 9.3.1 Numeric fields
text:
Calculating
You use numeric fields in a calculation in the same way. The layer states contains the population of each state in 1990 and 2010. On the previous page we already gave the example of how "POP2010" - "POP1990" calculates the population growth of each state. For Texas the expression becomes 25268418 - 17059805, which gives 8 208 613. Store the result in a new field POP_GROWTH of type Integer (32 bit).

title: 9.3.1 Numeric fields
text:
One-time calculations and virtual fields
A calculation with the Field Calculator is by default a one-time operation. The fields involved are not linked to each other, unlike cells in Excel that use formulas. So if you change POP1990 or POP2010, POP_GROWTH will not be updated.
If you want POP_GROWTH to follow such changes, tick Create virtual field in the Field Calculator, above Output field name. QGIS then recalculates the values whenever needed.
The downside is that a virtual field is not stored in the data source, but in the project. Other programs do not see it. To use it in another project, copy the layer to that project or save the layer style.

title: 9.3.2 Text fields
text:
In addition to numeric attribute fields, you can also use text fields in an expression. The following example uses the same vector layer of US cities as on the previous page.
The STATE_ABBR field contains the abbreviation of the state in which each city is located (for example, TX for Texas). To select features based on this field, double-click it under Fields and Values (B), similar to what you did for numeric fields.

When you select a field, QGIS lets you retrieve either all its unique values (All Unique) or a sample of values (10 Samples) (C). These values appear in an overview. Double-click a value to add it to your expression. Adding values this way is useful because it avoids typing errors. In our example we want to select all cities in Texas, so we add an = sign after the field name and then double-click TX. This gives "STATE_ABBR" = 'TX'.
Notice the quotation marks around TX. In QGIS expressions, text values must always be enclosed in single quotation marks. Without them, the expression is invalid and QGIS displays an error message.
It is important to mind the difference between single and double quotation marks:

Double quotation marks (" ") refer to a field.
Single quotation marks (' ') refer to a text value.
Numbers do not need quotation marks.







Always use straight quotation marks (" and '), as on your keyboard. Curly quotation marks (“ ” ‘ ’), which word processors insert automatically, do not work in QGIS.



When you use an equals sign (=), you only select the features whose value matches the given value exactly. Below you can see how to search more freely.



QGIS lets you use wildcards or ignore the difference between uppercase and lowercase letters. For this you do not use an equals sign in the expression but the operator LIKE or ILIKE:

LIKE takes uppercase and lowercase letters into account.
ILIKE ignores the difference between uppercase and lowercase letters.

A wildcard is a special character that can be used as a substitute for other characters in a text. It allows you to search for patterns instead of exact matches.
For example, Google uses * as a wildcard. However, this does not work in QGIS. Instead, QGIS uses two different wildcard characters:

The percent sign (%) stands for any number of characters, including none.
The underscore (_) stands for exactly one character.

The wildcards are written within the text string, that is, within the single quotation marks.
Some examples:

"NAME" LIKE '___' (three consecutive underscores) returns every city whose name consists of exactly three characters (e.g. Ada, Roy, Rye).
"NAME" LIKE 'San %' returns all cities whose name starts with ‘San’ and a space (e.g. San Antonio, San Jose). It does not matter how many characters follow.
"NAME" LIKE '%ville' works the other way round: it returns all cities whose name ends in ‘ville’ (e.g. Jacksonville, Louisville).
"CLASS" LIKE 'city%' returns all places whose class starts with ‘city’ (the field CLASS gives the type of place: city, town, village…). That can be just ‘city’, but also ‘city and borough’ (Juneau, Alaska). In this way you also find variants that you would miss with =.
"NAME" LIKE '%port%' returns the cities with ‘port’ in their name (e.g. Bridgeport, Newport Beach).
"NAME" ILIKE '%port%' also finds the names with a capital P (e.g. Port Hueneme, Porterville).
"NAME" LIKE '__n%ville' combines both wildcards: it returns all cities whose third character is an n and whose name ends in ‘ville’ (e.g. Danville, Huntsville). It does not matter which two characters come first, nor how many characters come between the n and ‘ville’.








For text fields, the Field Filter of the attribute table (section 8.2) uses ILIKE with a % wildcard on both sides. When you type port in the filter box of the field NAME, QGIS filters with "NAME" ILIKE '%port%'. That is why it ignores the difference between uppercase and lowercase letters and also finds names that only contain the text.

title: 9.3.2 Text fields
text:
In addition to numeric attribute fields, you can also use text fields in an expression. The following example uses the same vector layer of US cities as on the previous page.
The STATE_ABBR field contains the abbreviation of the state in which each city is located (for example, TX for Texas). To select features based on this field, double-click it under Fields and Values (B), similar to what you did for numeric fields.

When you select a field, QGIS lets you retrieve either all its unique values (All Unique) or a sample of values (10 Samples) (C). These values appear in an overview. Double-click a value to add it to your expression. Adding values this way is useful because it avoids typing errors. In our example we want to select all cities in Texas, so we add an = sign after the field name and then double-click TX. This gives "STATE_ABBR" = 'TX'.
Notice the quotation marks around TX. In QGIS expressions, text values must always be enclosed in single quotation marks. Without them, the expression is invalid and QGIS displays an error message.
It is important to mind the difference between single and double quotation marks:

Double quotation marks (" ") refer to a field.
Single quotation marks (' ') refer to a text value.
Numbers do not need quotation marks.







Always use straight quotation marks (" and '), as on your keyboard. Curly quotation marks (“ ” ‘ ’), which word processors insert automatically, do not work in QGIS.



When you use an equals sign (=), you only select the features whose value matches the given value exactly. Below you can see how to search more freely.



QGIS lets you use wildcards or ignore the difference between uppercase and lowercase letters. For this you do not use an equals sign in the expression but the operator LIKE or ILIKE:

LIKE takes uppercase and lowercase letters into account.
ILIKE ignores the difference between uppercase and lowercase letters.

A wildcard is a special character that can be used as a substitute for other characters in a text. It allows you to search for patterns instead of exact matches.
For example, Google uses * as a wildcard. However, this does not work in QGIS. Instead, QGIS uses two different wildcard characters:

The percent sign (%) stands for any number of characters, including none.
The underscore (_) stands for exactly one character.

The wildcards are written within the text string, that is, within the single quotation marks.
Some examples:

"NAME" LIKE '___' (three consecutive underscores) returns every city whose name consists of exactly three characters (e.g. Ada, Roy, Rye).
"NAME" LIKE 'San %' returns all cities whose name starts with ‘San’ and a space (e.g. San Antonio, San Jose). It does not matter how many characters follow.
"NAME" LIKE '%ville' works the other way round: it returns all cities whose name ends in ‘ville’ (e.g. Jacksonville, Louisville).
"CLASS" LIKE 'city%' returns all places whose class starts with ‘city’ (the field CLASS gives the type of place: city, town, village…). That can be just ‘city’, but also ‘city and borough’ (Juneau, Alaska). In this way you also find variants that you would miss with =.
"NAME" LIKE '%port%' returns the cities with ‘port’ in their name (e.g. Bridgeport, Newport Beach).
"NAME" ILIKE '%port%' also finds the names with a capital P (e.g. Port Hueneme, Porterville).
"NAME" LIKE '__n%ville' combines both wildcards: it returns all cities whose third character is an n and whose name ends in ‘ville’ (e.g. Danville, Huntsville). It does not matter which two characters come first, nor how many characters come between the n and ‘ville’.








For text fields, the Field Filter of the attribute table (section 8.2) uses ILIKE with a % wildcard on both sides. When you type port in the filter box of the field NAME, QGIS filters with "NAME" ILIKE '%port%'. That is why it ignores the difference between uppercase and lowercase letters and also finds names that only contain the text.

title: 9.3.2 Text fields
text:
Calculating
In the Field Calculator you can also calculate text values, such as manipulating existing text values (e.g. converting lower case to upper case) or combining values from different fields. In its simplest form your expression can be just a fixed text. In that case the ‘calculation’ simply takes the text as it is and writes it to the attribute field. Remember that, just as in a query, you write text values between single quotation marks.

In the example above, the expression 'Democrats' fills the field MAYOR_PARTY with this text for each feature it is applied to. Because Only update 4 selected feature(s) is ticked, the expression is applied only to the four selected cities.
Functions that actually transform a text are covered in 9.3.4 Text and math functions.

title: 9.3.3 NULL values
text:
An attribute field does not always contain a value. This can happen with both text and numeric fields. In the attribute table, QGIS displays such an empty value as NULL. This is not the same as 0, FALSE or an empty text string. NULL is simply nothing.










It is perfectly normal for some features to have empty attribute fields. However, it is important to know how to query these fields and how QGIS handles NULL values in expressions and calculations.

To check whether a field contains an empty value, use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. For example, in the layer states the field REPR2010 contains the number of seats of each state in the House of Representatives in 2010. "REPR2010" IS NULL selects all features where this field has no value. This is the only correct way to check for NULL values.
A comparison with NULL always returns NULL. QGIS treats this as ‘not true’. So, for example, comparisons such as NULL < 5, NULL = 0 or even NULL = NULL do not return TRUE. This is why "REPR2010" = NULL does not select features with an empty value.
You cannot perform calculations with NULL values. For example, NULL + 3 and NULL - 3 both return NULL. In the Field Calculator, "REPR2010" - "REPR1990" gives the change in the number of seats of every state over 20 years. The District of Columbia and the territories have no seats, so for them the result is NULL.
To remove values from your attribute table, use the Field Calculator and simply write NULL to the fields.

There is a method to change all NULLs in a field to another value in one go. We cover this on the next page.

title: 9.3.4 Text and math functions
text:
Functions let you do more with your data than simply read or compare it. They are ready-made operations that take an input, such as a field value, and return a result based on it. You can use them for example to change text values, round a number or compare a value with the average across all features.
A simple example: in a layer containing the major cities of the United States, upper("NAME") converts the name of every city to capital letters. For Chicago, it gives CHICAGO.
QGIS provides many functions for working with text, numbers, geometries and other types of data. You can find them in the central panel (B) of the Expression Builder and the Field Calculator, together with the available fields. Most functions follow the same basic syntax: a function name followed by one or more arguments in brackets.
function_name(argument_1, argument_2)
An argument is the input a function needs to perform its operation.
Remember that QGIS evaluates an expression for each feature separately. When you use a field as an argument, QGIS uses the field value of the current feature. You can also enter a fixed value, which QGIS then uses for every feature.

title: 9.3.4 Text and math functions
text:
Syntax and arguments
The arguments a function requires depend on what it does. Some functions expect a single value, while others need several arguments of different types, such as numbers or geometries. When a function requires multiple arguments, separate them with commas and pay attention to their order.
You do not need to memorise these requirements. The function documentation in QGIS tells you exactly what each function needs (C).

Documentation
For each function the documentation shows what it does (C1), its syntax (C2), the required type of each argument (C3) and examples showing how to use it and what output to expect (C4).

You can use this information whenever you are unfamiliar with a function. Let’s look at three examples.

1. upper() – changing text to capital letters
The function upper() requires one argument: a text value (string). It returns that text in capital letters.



2. round() – rounding a number
The function round() requires a number. You can also provide a second argument to specify the number of decimal places.
In the syntax, square brackets [ ] indicate an optional argument. If you leave it out, QGIS rounds to a whole number.
For Chicago, round("POPULATION" / 1000000, 1) returns 2.7. The population is first converted to millions and then rounded to one decimal place.



3. replace() – replacing part of a text
The function replace() requires three text arguments:

the original text;
the part you want to replace;
the replacement text.

For St. Louis, replace("NAME", 'St.', 'Saint') returns Saint Louis.
The documentation also shows another version of this function that uses a map. We will not use that version here.

You can use the function list to explore what QGIS has to offer. If you know what you want to do, type a related term, such as average or round, in the search box at the top of the function list (B). Browse the results and use the documentation to check what each function does and whether it suits your needs.
This means you can find and learn to use almost any function yourself. In the following sections, we will look at a selection of functions that you are likely to use regularly.

title: 9.3.4 Text and math functions
text:
String functions
String functions work with text values. You can find them in the String group of the central function list (B).

Here are some common operations, with examples using the city of St. Louis.

Changing the case: upper(text) converts a text to uppercase, lower(text) to lowercase, and title(text) capitalises the first letter of each word. lower("NAME") gives st. louis, title('st. louis') gives St. Louis.
Cleaning up a text: trim(text) removes spaces at the start and end of a text. trim('  St. Louis  ') gives St. Louis without the spaces.
Changing a text: replace(text, before, after) replaces part of a text with another text. replace("NAME", 'St.', 'Saint') gives Saint Louis.
Combining texts: concat(text1, text2, …) joins texts into one text. concat("NAME", ' (', "STATE_ABBR", ')') gives St. Louis (MO).
Counting characters: length(text) returns the number of characters in a text. length("NAME") gives 9.

You can also use the result of a function in a condition. For example length("NAME") > 20 identifies cities with names longer than 20 characters.

title: 9.3.4 Text and math functions
text:
Math functions
Math functions perform calculations on numerical values. You can find them in the Math group of the central function list (B).

A common use is rounding numbers. The following examples use Chicago, which has a population of 2 746 388.

Rounding to a specified number of decimals: round(number, decimals) rounds a number to the number of decimal places you specify. For example round("POPULATION" / 1000000, 1) returns 2.7.
Rounding up: ceil(number) rounds a number up to the nearest whole number. For example ceil("POPULATION" / 1000000) returns 3.
Rounding down: floor(number) rounds a number down to the nearest whole number. For example floor("POPULATION" / 1000000) returns 2.

title: 9.3.4 Text and math functions
text:
Aggregate functions
Sometimes you want to compare a feature’s value with values from all other features in the layer. Aggregate functions let you do this. You can find them in the Aggregates group. Common examples are mean(), sum() and maximum().
Unlike the functions we have seen so far, aggregate functions calculate a result using values from multiple features. Let’s look at an example.
Suppose you want to compare each city’s population with the average population of all cities in the layer. You can do this with the following expression:
"POPULATION" - mean("POPULATION")
In the Field Calculator you can store the result in a new field, here POP_DIFF.

Notice that the field POPULATION appears twice in the expression, but it is used differently each time.
Before the minus sign, QGIS uses the population of the current feature. Inside mean(), it calculates the average population across all features. The expression therefore subtracts the overall average from each city’s population.

title: 9.3.4 Text and math functions
text:
Replacing NULL values
As you learned on the previous page, attribute fields can contain NULL values, meaning that no value is available. This can prevent you from performing calculations or comparisons with those values. Sometimes, you may want to replace missing values with a value such as 0. QGIS provides the function coalesce() for this purpose.

Its documentation explains that you can provide any number of arguments. The function returns the first argument that is not NULL.
Consider a layer of the US states, with the number of seats each had in the House of Representatives in 2010 stored in the REPR2010 field. For the District of Columbia and the territories, this field is NULL. You can use coalesce("REPR2010", 0) to replace these NULL values with 0 while leaving existing values unchanged.
You can also use coalesce() in calculations. For example coalesce("REPR2010", 0) - coalesce("REPR1990", 0) calculates the change in the number of seats between 1990 and 2010, treating NULL values as 0. This returns 0 instead of NULL for the District of Columbia.
You have now explored several functions for working with text and numbers. Later in this chapter you learn the functions for geometries and for other layers and features.

title: 9.4 Logical operators
text:
Points to note

On both sides of an AND or OR operator QGIS always expects a complete expression that can stand on its own and whose result can be true (TRUE / 1) or false (FALSE / 0). This also applies if both conditions refer to the same field. In other words, "STATE_ABBR" = 'CA' OR 'TX' will not give you the desired result, while "STATE_ABBR" = 'CA' OR "STATE_ABBR" = 'TX' will.
If you use the NOT operator in combination with an AND or OR operator, the inversion only applies to the part of the expression directly after NOT, not to the whole expression. To keep your expression clear, it helps to put that part between brackets. If you want to invert the whole expression, the brackets are required. For example, NOT ("STATE_ABBR" = 'CA') AND "POPULATION" > 500000 inverts only the state condition, while NOT ("STATE_ABBR" = 'CA' AND "POPULATION" > 500000) inverts the whole expression.
With OR, QGIS evaluates the part before and the part after OR separately. If one of the two parts is TRUE, that is enough, even if the other part is NULL. "POPULATION" > 50000 OR "STATE_ABBR" = 'CA' therefore also selects a city in California whose population is empty (NULL). With AND such a city is of course not selected (see NULL values).

title: 9.5.1 Using a geometry in expressions
text:
On the previous pages you learned how to query features by their attribute values. In this section, we look at how to query features based on their geometry.
Before we begin, let’s clarify what we mean by a geometry in GIS. A geometry describes the location and shape of a feature. It consists of two elements: a geometry type ((multi-)point, line or polygon) and a set of coordinates. A point has one pair of coordinates, a line or polygon several pairs. 






A multi-geometry consists of several separate parts. For example, a country with islands can be represented as one feature with a multipolygon geometry: one polygon for the mainland and one for each island. All parts of a multi-geometry have the same geometry type.



In an expression you can calculate various properties of a geometry, such as its area, length or number of parts.
To work with geometries in expressions, QGIS provides the following elements:

The variable @geometry, which retrieves the geometry of the current feature.
The geometry functions $area, $length and $perimeter, which calculate common geometric properties of the current feature without requiring any additional input.
A wide range of other functions for working with geometries. Most of these take one or more geometries as arguments. For example, distance(geometry1, geometry2) calculates the minimum distance between two geometries.

title: 9.5.1 Using a geometry in expressions
text:
The variable @geometry
@geometry retrieves the geometry of the current feature. It works much like a field name between double quotation marks: a field name retrieves the attribute value of each feature, while @geometry retrieves its geometry.
In QGIS the @ sign identifies variables. You can find @geometry in the list of Variables (B) in the Expression Builder.

On its own, @geometry is rarely useful. Its strength lies in combining it with geometric functions, which we discuss on the next page.

title: 9.5.2 Geometric functions
text: Earlier in this chapter, you learned how to use functions to work with text and numbers. QGIS also provides many functions for working with geometries. Generally they work in the same way as the functions you have already encountered: you write the function name and add the arguments behind it between brackets. There are, however, also three special functions with a different syntax. Let’s take a closer look at these first.

title: 9.5.2 Geometric functions
text:
$area, $length and $perimeter
QGIS provides three distinctive functions whose names start with a $ sign. Unlike other functions, they do not require any arguments: they always work on the current feature. That is why they are written without brackets. These functions calculate common geometric properties of the current feature:

$area: the area of a polygon
$length: the length of a line
$perimeter: the perimeter of a polygon

You can find them under Geometry in the central list of the Expression Builder (B), along with many other ‘traditional’ functions. As you already learned, you can find more information about each of them in the panel on the right (C).
With the default project settings, these functions take the Earth’s curvature into account. They also return their results in metres (square metres for $area), even when the layer uses a geographic CRS such as WGS 84, where coordinates are expressed in degrees. We explain this in more detail on the next page.


Querying example
Suppose you apply the expression shown above, $area > 300000000000, to a layer containing the states of the United States. As QGIS loops over the features, it calculates the area of each current feature and checks whether it is larger than 300 000 km². As a result five states are selected: Alaska, Texas, California, Montana and New Mexico.


Calculating example
You can also use the functions $area, $length and $perimeter in the Field Calculator.

The same layer of the United States also contains population figures for different years. Suppose you want to calculate the population density of the different states for the year 1990. You can do this with the expression shown above, "POP1990" / ($area / 1000000). For each feature QGIS takes the attribute value from the field POP1990 and divides it by the calculated area of its geometry. Dividing by 1 000 000 converts square metres to square kilometres.

title: 9.5.2 Geometric functions
text:
Geometric functions with arguments

Commonly used geometric functions
You can use these functions to retrieve geometric properties, check how geometries relate to each other in space, or even create new geometries on the fly. You find these functions in the central list (B), under Geometry. Most of them expect one or more geometries as arguments. Some examples:

area(geometry), length(geometry), perimeter(geometry): calculate the area, length or perimeter of a geometry. Unlike $area, $length and $perimeter, these functions require a geometry as an argument.
distance(geometry1, geometry2): calculates the minimum distance between two geometries.
crosses(geometry1, geometry2): checks whether two geometries cross each other. It returns TRUE if they do and FALSE if they do not.
make_point(number1, number2), make_line(point1, point2), make_polygon(line): create a new point from a pair of coordinates, a line from two or more points, or a polygon from a closed line.
centroid(geometry): returns the centroid (geometric centre) of a geometry as a point.
x(geometry), y(geometry): return the x or y coordinate of a point geometry. For a line or polygon, they return the x or y coordinate of its centroid.
x_max(geometry), x_min(geometry), y_max(geometry), y_min(geometry): return the largest or smallest x or y coordinate of a geometry. In a geographic CRS such as WGS 84, x is the longitude and y the latitude, both expressed in degrees. In a projected CRS such as Belgian Lambert 72, x and y are coordinates expressed in metres, representing positions east and north of a fixed origin.







These are only a few examples. Browse the group Geometry in the Expression Builder to discover more.





Syntax and arguments
In Text and math functions you learned how to read the documentation of a function. This of course also applies to geometric functions. The main difference from the functions on that page lies in the type of arguments they require and the type of output they return: for most geometric functions, one or both of these are geometries. To use the geometry of the current feature while querying or calculating, you can use the variable @geometry, as you learned in Using a geometry in expressions. Let’s look at three examples.
centroid() requires one argument: a geometry. It returns a point geometry representing the centroid of the input geometry.

Other functions require multiple arguments, separated by commas. These arguments are not necessarily geometries. For example, make_point() requires two numbers: the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate.

distance() requires two geometries and returns the minimum distance between them. For a polygon and a point, for example, this is the distance from the point to the nearest edge of the polygon. Between two points, it is simply the distance from one point to the other.

title: 9.5.2 Geometric functions
text:
Nesting
The output of one function can be used as the input for another function. This is called nesting: one function is placed inside another. Let’s look at an example.
Suppose you have a layer containing the Belgian municipalities. You want to select only those municipalities that meet both of the following conditions:

their area is larger than 100 km²
the centroid of the municipality is located less than 100 km from the city centre of Ghent

For the first condition, you need to calculate the area of each municipality and compare it with 100 km². For the second, you need to calculate the centroid of each municipality and measure its distance from the centre of Ghent. You can use functions to calculate the areas and centroids, and to create a point representing the centre of Ghent. All of this can be combined in a single expression:

Look up the functions used here in the Expression Builder and read their documentation to understand exactly what happens.
The coordinates 105000, 194000 represent the centre of Ghent in the layer’s CRS: BD72 / Belgian Lambert 72 (EPSG:31370). This projected CRS uses metres as its coordinate units. We looked up these coordinates and use them as fixed values in the expression.
In this example, distance() does not use the municipality geometries directly. Instead, it uses their centroids and a point created with make_point(). This means that it measures the distance from the centroid of each municipality to the centre of Ghent, rather than the distance from the municipality’s nearest edge.

title: 9.5.3 Units of measurement
text:
When using geometric functions, it is important to understand which units they use and how the calculations are performed. This can differ from one function to another. The documentation gives you this information.
Some functions seem to do the same thing. You may have noticed on the previous page that we gave both $area and area() as examples to calculate the area of a feature. Still, these variants can give different results, because the calculation is done differently.

title: 9.5.3 Units of measurement
text:
$area, $length and $perimeter
$area, $length and $perimeter take the Earth’s curvature into account by using the reference ellipsoid defined in the project properties (Project ▸ Properties… ▸ General). They return their results in the measurement units set there (by default metres and square metres), even when the layer uses a geographic CRS such as WGS 84, where coordinates are expressed in degrees.
By default, QGIS uses the ellipsoid associated with the project’s CRS. For a project in Belgian Lambert 72 (EPSG:31370), for example, this is the International 1924 ellipsoid, while a project in WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) uses the WGS 84 ellipsoid. If no ellipsoid is set (None / Planimetric), the calculations are planimetric. By default, the measurement units are metres and square metres, but you can change them. You could even choose units that are rarely used in practice, such as square degrees.






The default unit for areas is therefore the square metre. This works well for smaller areas, but for large areas such as countries, it results in very large numbers. In such cases, it is often more convenient to divide the result by 1 000 000 to express it in square kilometres (1 km² = 1000 m × 1000 m).

title: 9.5.3 Units of measurement
text:
area(), length() and perimeter()
area(@geometry), length(@geometry) and perimeter(@geometry) calculate the area, length and perimeter directly from the geometry’s coordinates, using the CRS of the layer. Pay attention: if your layer uses a CRS in degrees, such as WGS 84, the area is expressed in square degrees, a number that means little. When using these functions, make sure that the layer uses a CRS that is appropriate for the type of measurement and the region concerned. For area calculations, use an equal-area CRS, such as ETRS89-extended / LAEA Europe (EPSG:3035) for Europe. For length and perimeter calculations, choose a suitable projected CRS that minimises distortion in the region concerned. If your layer is not yet in a suitable CRS, you can always reproject it, for example with the tool Reproject layer (see Explicit transformations).

title: 9.5.3 Units of measurement
text:
Comparison









$area, $length, $perimeter
area(@geometry), length(@geometry), perimeter(@geometry)




Calculation method
Uses the project ellipsoid by default. If none is set, calculations are planimetric.
Always planimetric, using the CRS of the geometry.


Units
Uses the measurement units set in the project properties.
Uses the units of the geometry’s CRS (e.g. m² for a projected CRS in metres, or degrees² for WGS 84).


Suitable for
Ellipsoidal calculations are suitable for measuring areas and distances over large regions. They also work well for smaller regions.
Suitable when the geometry uses a projected CRS with limited distortion for the region and type of measurement concerned.


To avoid large deviations
Choose an appropriate ellipsoid in the project properties.
Use a suitable projected CRS with limited distortion in the region concerned.



Consider a layer containing the territory of Belgium as a single feature. The following examples assume that the project ellipsoid is set to match the ellipsoid associated with the layer’s CRS.

The layer is stored in WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) coordinates:

$area gives about 30 692 km².
area(@geometry) gives about 3.90 square degrees, a number that means little.

The same territory is stored in Belgian Lambert 72 (EPSG:31370) coordinates:

$area gives about 30 692 km².
area(@geometry) gives about 30 690 km².


In a projected CRS with metres as its coordinate units, the two functions therefore give almost the same result, with a difference of about 0.01%. This small difference is due to distortion introduced by the projection (see Projection distortions in chapter 5). The exact results depend on the geometry and the settings used.

title: 9.6 Other layers and features
text:
In Geometric functions we applied geometric functions to the geometry of the current feature. Sometimes we combined it with something derived from that geometry (such as its centroid) or with a point created on the fly (such as the centre of Ghent). However, these functions can also be applied to any other geometry.
We build on the example in Nesting to show why this can be useful. There we used a fixed threshold to select municipalities that are larger than 100 km². We now want to make this condition relative rather than absolute: instead of using a fixed area as a threshold, we want to select municipalities that are larger than Ghent itself. The expression therefore compares two areas:
To calculate the latter, you need access to Ghent’s geometry. To do this, QGIS offers several functions and variables for retrieving specific features, including their geometry and attributes. The following sections introduce these.

title: 9.6 Other layers and features
text:
Retrieving a specific feature

Layers
The first step is to identify the layer that contains the feature. Often that is the layer you are writing the expression for, but you can also use features from any other layer loaded in your project.

@layer is a variable that refers to the current layer, that is, the layer for which you are writing the expression. You find it under Variables.
The Map Layers section (B) lists all the layers in your project, the current layer included. If you double-click a layer name there, QGIS adds its layer ID to your expression. This ID is a text string enclosed in single quotation marks. It uniquely identifies the layer within the project, even if other layers have the same name.




Features
Once you have identified the layer, you can retrieve a specific feature from it. For this, you can use the following functions under Record and Attributes (B):

get_feature(layer, attribute_field_name, value) retrieves only the first feature in the specified layer whose attribute in the given field matches the specified value. Even if several features match, you get only one.
get_feature_by_id(layer, id) retrieves the feature with the specified feature ID from the layer.

The documentation of get_feature() shows what you need:



Geometry and attributes
Remember that a feature is not the same as a geometry. A feature consists of a geometry and its associated attributes. The geometry describes the feature’s shape and location. Geometric functions such as area() operate on the geometry, not on the feature itself.
Once you have retrieved a feature, two functions give you access to its geometry and its attribute values:

geometry(feature) returns the geometry of the feature (under Geometry).
attribute(feature, attribute_field_name) returns the value of the feature in this attribute field (under Record and Attributes).







The get_feature() function returns a complete feature, including its geometry and attributes. That is why you need to wrap it in geometry() before you can use it in functions that need a geometry as input, such as area().

title: 9.6 Other layers and features
text:
Examples

Municipalities larger than Ghent
We first focus on the area of Ghent. To calculate it, we can use the following expression:

Study how the different functions are nested here:

First, we retrieve the feature representing Ghent using get_feature(). We need to specify the layer (here, the current layer, @layer), an attribute field and a value to search for. In this layer, only one municipality has the name Gent (the Dutch name used in the dataset), so we use the field NAME and the value 'Gent'.
The function above returns a feature. To calculate its area, we first extract its geometry using geometry().
Finally, area() calculates the area of this geometry. It uses a planimetric calculation, but because the layer uses BD72 / Belgian Lambert 72 (EPSG:31370), the result is very reliable for Belgium.

Finally, we can bring this calculation into the expression we started with above. This is the final result:

Three municipalities with their centroid within 100 km of Ghent’s city centre have a larger area than Ghent itself: Antwerp, Beveren-Kruibeke-Zwijndrecht and Tournai.

You can use a similar expression in the Field Calculator. For example, the expression distance(centroid(@geometry), centroid(geometry(get_feature(@layer, 'NAME', 'Gent')))) / 1000 can write for each municipality the distance in km from its centroid to the centroid of Ghent to the attribute table.


Cities north of the Ohio
In the Ghent example, get_feature() retrieved a feature from the current layer (@layer). It can also retrieve features from other layers in your project. Suppose you want to select all major cities of the United States that lie (directly) north of the Ohio River. You make the selection among the cities, but the Ohio itself is stored in a separate layer of major rivers.










How can you identify these cities? Draw a line due south from each city and check whether it crosses the Ohio River. If it does, the city lies north of the river. The line needs a starting point (the city itself) and an endpoint far enough south to extend beyond the river. We use a point at the same longitude as the city and at the latitude of the southernmost point of the Ohio River. QGIS can do all of this in one expression:
crosses(geometry(get_feature('major_rivers', 'NAME', 'Ohio')), make_line(@geometry, make_point(x(@geometry), y_min(geometry(get_feature('major_rivers', 'NAME', 'Ohio'))))))
The expression retrieves the Ohio River from the major_rivers layer, constructs a line from the current city to a point due south of it, and checks whether this line crosses the river.






Make sure that both layers use the same coordinate reference system, so that their geometries can be compared correctly. QGIS does not reproject the geometry that get_feature() retrieves from another layer. Here both major_cities and major_rivers are in WGS 84 (EPSG:4326).




For clarity, the image below shows the auxiliary lines that you create. When you apply this expression in normal circumstances, these lines remain purely virtual, so you will not see them.

* In the maps on this page, the selected points have a black outline for clarity. You can change the look of selected features in Layer Properties ▸ Rendering ▸ Selections ▸ Override symbol for selected features.

title: 9.7 Labelling and styling with expressions
text: In the previous sections you learned how expressions can be used for calculations and queries. However, they can also be used to control how features are displayed on the map, for example through labelling and styling. You can compose the text of a label with an expression, and, as with queries, you can define conditions and apply a particular label or style to the features that meet them.

title: 9.7 Labelling and styling with expressions
text:
Compose the label text
So far, we always labelled a layer based on a single field. However, you can also compose the label text with an expression. When you open the Labels tab in the Layer Properties, you will notice that next to the drop-down list where you select the attribute field (Value), there is also a button . Click it to open the Expression Builder. Here you can compose an expression that returns a value (usually a text), which is then used as the label of each feature. Take for example a layer of US cities with a field for the name of each city (NAME) and a field with the abbreviation of the state it lies in (STATE_ABBR). If you want to label each city with its name followed by the state between brackets, such as Chicago (IL), you can use the expression concat("NAME", ' (', "STATE_ABBR", ')'), which you already saw in Text and math functions.

title: 9.7 Labelling and styling with expressions
text:
Rules
In the example above all features of the layer are labelled in the same way, just as in chapter 4. They all use the same field or expression to determine the label text, and the same label style is applied to all of them. Of course you have also learned how to use Categorized or Graduated symbology to vary the appearance of features, but these approaches assign each feature exactly one symbol, based on the value of a single field.
However, sometimes you want more control over how individual features are displayed. For example you may want to label only the largest cities and vary the font size according to their population. Or you may want to combine several conditions to determine the symbol used for a feature.
Rule-based styling makes this possible: it allows you to create rules in which you define a condition and link it to a specific style. QGIS then applies that style to all features that meet the condition.
Rules work in the same way for labels and for symbology. Below we first explain how you create them. Then two examples show a complete map, one for labels and one for symbology.

Rule-based labeling and symbology
In the layer’s Layer Properties, open the Symbology tab and select Rule-based at the top (A1). For labels, you open the Labels tab and select Rule-based Labeling in the same place.










The large empty area (A2) is the rule overview. It is initially empty because no rules have been defined. Click the green plus symbol at the bottom of the window (A3) to create a new rule. This opens the Edit Rule window.


Rule editor
The rule editor has two main sections below the Label field (where you can enter a descriptive name for the rule, B1):

the condition that identifies the features to which the rule applies (B2)
the style that determines how these features are displayed (B3)












Condition (B2)
The condition goes in the Filter field and takes the form of an expression. Expressions can be typed directly into this field or entered through the full Expression Builder, opened with the button  (B4). The expression must return either TRUE or FALSE. Typical examples include comparisons or functions such as crosses(). As in the previous sections, QGIS evaluates the expression for each feature and applies the rule to those for which it returns TRUE.
Instead of a condition, you can also choose Else (Catch-all for other features, just below the Filter field). Such a rule applies to all features that match none of the other rules. Without an Else rule, those features get no label or symbol.


Style (B3)
In this section you determine the symbol (marker, colour, size…) or the label style (label text, font, colour…) that the features meeting the condition receive. It looks and works exactly like the settings of Single Symbol symbology and Single Labels respectively.
Click OK to save the rule. All the rules you created are shown in the rule overview (A2). To edit a rule, double-click it. You can delete a rule with the red minus symbol (A3).



Features that meet several rules
When using rule-based symbology, a feature that matches several rules gets the symbol defined by each of them. QGIS draws these symbols on top of each other, in the order of the rule list. This means that the last rule in the list is drawn on top. If a symbol covers the symbols below it, those are no longer visible.

title: 9.7 Labelling and styling with expressions
text:
Examples

Labelling the largest cities
Consider a point layer containing the major cities of the United States. The aim is to label only the most populated cities, with the label size reflecting their population. We therefore need three rules, one for each group of cities to be labelled:


Rule 1

condition: "POPULATION" > 2000000
label text: concat("NAME", ' (', round("POPULATION" / 1000000, 1), ' M)')
style: 20 pt, black

Rule 2

condition: "POPULATION" > 1000000 AND "POPULATION" <= 2000000
label text: NAME
style: 14 pt, dark grey

Rule 3

condition: "POPULATION" > 500000 AND "POPULATION" <= 1000000
label text: NAME
style: 9 pt, grey



For the first rule, the label text is an expression instead of the field NAME (see Compose the label text), so that these cities also show their population in millions, for example New York (8.8 M). In the next two rules we use the <= operator to include cities with exactly 2 000 000 or 1 000 000 inhabitants respectively. Cities with fewer than 500 000 inhabitants match none of the rules, so they remain unlabelled.
When you have created the rules and click OK at the bottom of the Layer Properties, you immediately see the result in your map canvas: only the largest cities are labelled, and the larger the city, the larger its label.












Seats in the House of Representatives
Above, each rule used a simple condition on one attribute value. Just as in other expressions, you can also combine several fields in a rule and use functions, such as the aggregate functions mean(), maximum() and minimum().
Consider a polygon layer containing the US states, with the number of seats in the House of Representatives (REPR1990, REPR2010) and the population (POP1990, POP2010) of every state. The map should show three aspects of representation:

Change in seats: did the state gain seats between 1990 and 2010, lose seats, or keep the same number? Each outcome gets its own fill colour.
Change in relative representation: did the number of seats per inhabitant increase or decrease between 1990 and 2010, relative to the average state? States where it increased are hatched.
Extremes in 2010: which state had the most seats per inhabitant, and which had the fewest? These two states get a coloured outline.

Note that with these criteria a state can meet several conditions. Every state that is hatched or outlined, for example, also has a fill colour. A classification based on a single attribute, such as Categorized symbology, is not well suited to this task, because it gives every feature exactly one symbol. With rule-based symbology every characteristic gets its own rule.
We build this map in two parts: first the fill colours, then the hatching and the outlines.

Fill colours
In the Symbology tab, select Rule-based and add the rules one by one with the green plus symbol. The rule overview shows the four rules of the first part, each with its filter expression and its colour.


Rule 1

condition: "REPR2010" > "REPR1990"
style: green fill

Rule 2

condition: "REPR2010" < "REPR1990"
style: orange fill

Rule 3

condition: "REPR2010" = "REPR1990"
style: beige fill

Rule 4

condition: Else
style: grey fill



Rule 4 is an Else rule for the features with NULL values, for example the District of Columbia and the territories.










The map after the first part: every state has exactly one fill colour.


Hatching and outlines
Now add three more rules. Each of them only adds something on top of the fill colour.


Rule 5

condition: "REPR2010" / "POP2010" / mean("REPR2010" / "POP2010") - "REPR1990" / "POP1990" / mean("REPR1990" / "POP1990") > 0
style: hatching, without a fill colour



In rule 5, "REPR2010" / "POP2010" calculates the number of seats per inhabitant in 2010. Dividing this value by the mean of the seats-per-inhabitant ratio across all states expresses it relative to the average state. The same calculation is made for 1990. The expression then subtracts the 1990 value from the 2010 value. A result greater than 0 means that the state’s relative representation increased.


Rule 6

condition: "REPR2010" / "POP2010" = maximum("REPR2010" / "POP2010")
style: blue outline, without a fill colour

Rule 7

condition: "REPR2010" / "POP2010" = minimum("REPR2010" / "POP2010")
style: red outline, without a fill colour



Rules 6 and 7 select the states with the most and the fewest seats per inhabitant in 2010.
With every rule we add, we may change the group of features that fall under the Else rule as well. Remember that Else applies to all features that match none of the other rules, also those defined after it. In our case it is hypothetically possible that a state with a NULL value for 1990 turns out to have the most seats per inhabitant in 2010. Because it would then match rule 6, it would lose its grey fill. Therefore it is necessary to replace the existing Else rule by a filter that describes the missing data:


Updated rule 4

condition: "REPR1990" IS NULL OR "REPR2010" IS NULL
style: grey fill



Keep in mind that states that meet several rules receive all the corresponding symbols, drawn on top of each other (see Features that meet several rules). Make sure you sort the rules logically in the rule overview: the fill colours at the top, the hatching and outlines below them, so that they are drawn on top of the fills.










The map after the second part. Every state has a fill colour, and the hatching and outlines lie on top of it.






You can now do Exercise 3, part C.
